seo.title: Karmic tail 15 17 20 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 15 17 20 compatibility: The Devil, The Star and Judgement — how a couple moves from a chain through openness to a family of its own.

title: Karmic tail 15-17-20 in compatibility: who belongs to whom
short: The Devil at the entry and the Last Judgement at the end — at first sight this is a tail about chains and verdicts. In fact the couple's tail 15-17-20 is the story of a single word: "belong". Two people enter their shared task through an attraction in which each wants to possess and to be possessed. They go through it by way of openness, where there is nothing left to hide. And the main task is to turn the two of them into a family in which they belong to each other without a chain.

paragraphs: In the third volume one of Pierre's brother Masons reveals to him a "prophecy". If French letters are written as numbers, the words L'Empereur Napoléon add up to 666, the number of the beast in the Apocalypse. Pierre tries his own name. Comte Pierre Besouhoff does not work. Le russe Besuhof gives 671: five too many, and five stands for the letter e. He drops it, "though incorrectly", gets L'russe Besuhof, exactly 666, and "this discovery excited him".

Then Tolstoy lists, in a single sentence, what is going on in Pierre's head: "His love for Natásha, Antichrist, Napoleon, the invasion, the comet, 666, L'Empereur Napoléon, and L'russe Besuhof—all this had to mature and culminate, to lift him out of that spellbound, petty sphere of Moscow habits in which he felt himself held captive" (translated by Louise and Aylmer Maude). The whole of tail 15-17-20 is in that sentence. In the tarot deck the beast of the Apocalypse is closest to the fifteenth card, The Devil. The comet is a star. And near the end of the Apocalypse comes the Last Judgement — exactly what Waite calls the twentieth card in his classic deck: The Last Judgment. In the first full draft of the novel, finished by the end of 1866, Pierre shows his figures to Natasha, and she answers: "Yes, it's frightening," she said, "and the comet" (our translation).

Tolstoy laughs at his hero: to reach the number he wanted, Pierre had to break the grammar. And the prophecy does not come true — Pierre never kills Napoleon. This article takes the opposite road. No letters are bent here: the three numbers come from two dates of birth, and the secret lies not in a prediction but in what the cards themselves are about. And if one reads the novel rather than Pierre's sums, the tail is already there, in order: two chains, a comet, a resurrection and a family.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — The Devil: two chains from one house
paragraphs: Pierre and Natasha enter their story unfree, and both chains are held by one family, the Kuragins. Pierre is married off to Hélène, Prince Vasili's daughter. Natasha is very nearly carried off by Hélène's brother Anatole, and it is Hélène herself who introduces them in her box at the opera: "Let me introduce my brother to you."

Tolstoy describes both captivities in the same words. Pierre, in the first volume: "between them there was no longer any barrier except the barrier of his own will". Natasha, in the second: "again she felt with horror that no barrier lay between him and her". Closeness arrives before knowledge — that is the first face of The Devil. Hélène's glance says it aloud: "Yes, I am a woman who may belong to anyone—to you too."

Then come details that are easy to miss. The first thing his bride asks of Pierre, right after the engagement, is: "Oh, take those off... those..." — his spectacles. He takes them off, and his eyes have "a frightened and inquiring look". Then he says "Je vous aime!", "remembering what has to be said at such moments: but his words sounded so weak that he felt ashamed of himself". A borrowed phrase in a borrowed language, said because it is what one says. Pierre talks himself round in the same way: "All this had to be and could not be otherwise." Years later, as a prisoner, he will see that when he married his wife "of his own free will as it had seemed to him—he had been no more free than now when they locked him up at night in a stable".

The Kuragin chain is forged out of an inheritance. Pierre is the illegitimate son of old Count Bezukhov. At the door of the dying man the family fights over a mosaic portfolio with the will in it, and Anna Mikhaylovna calls Pierre into a "family consultation". Pierre becomes the heir, and then Prince Vasili marries his daughter to him. In the book by Yuliana Lisovskaya on which the compatibility calculation is based, inheritance, kin and lawsuits within the family are themes of the twentieth energy. So from the first chapters Tolstoy ties the entry of the tail to its end.

For a couple, the entry M is the shared wish and the common language with which the task begins. With The Devil the wish is strong and bodily: no barriers, only us, to be someone's and to have someone of one's own. On the plus side Lisovskaya sees a passionate, vivid union in which each accepts the other's dark sides and forgives mistakes, and sometimes one helps the other out of a destructive story. Pierre does exactly that: he takes Natasha's letters back from Anatole and has him leave Moscow.

On the minus side the same wish becomes a chain. One of the two skips a night out with friends because "we're fine just the two of us", and a year later cannot remember when they last saw those friends. A quarrel ends not in a conversation but in making up in bed, and whatever caused it stays lying between them. A present instead of an apology. Jealousy counted as proof of love. Desires kept quiet in case the other takes fright and leaves. Lisovskaya ends her chapter on the fifteenth energy with a line: it teaches "that no one belongs to anyone".

In this couple The Devil is always made of two personal entries: The Lovers of one partner (6) and The Hermit of the other (9). One brings the readiness to fall in love and to choose, the other the depth of someone who lives in their own world and lets only one person in. Tolstoy seems to have handed out the roles by this formula: Natasha, quick to fall in love, and Pierre the Mason, a hermit with eternal questions. Together it becomes "you are my world". And a world for two easily turns into a locked room.

sections.h2: Middle of the task — The Star: a comet in the middle of the sky and of the novel
paragraphs: The evening after the business with Anatole. Natasha, grown thin, stands in the middle of the drawing room "just in the pose she used to stand in when she went to the middle of the ballroom to sing", and asks Pierre to tell Prince Andrew to forgive her. "All is over for me." Pierre answers: "Stop, stop! You have your whole life before you" — and then says something that surprises him: "If I were not myself, but the handsomest, cleverest, and best man in the world, and were free, I would this moment ask on my knees for your hand and your love!" "For the first time for many days Natásha wept tears of gratitude and tenderness."

Pierre goes out, throws open his bearskin coat in the frost, and above the Arbat Square he sees: "Almost in the center of it, above the Prechístenka Boulevard, surrounded and sprinkled on all sides by stars but distinguished from them all by its nearness to the earth, its white light, and its long uplifted tail, shone the enormous and brilliant comet of 1812—the comet which was said to portend all kinds of woes and the end of the world."

A star with a tail stands almost in the middle of the sky, and the scene itself stands in the middle of the novel: it closes the second of its four volumes. Exactly where The Star stands in this tail. And there is one more clue: the comet is supposed to foretell the end of the world, that is, the Last Judgement, the twentieth card. But Pierre is not afraid: "this comet fully responded to what was passing in his own softened and uplifted soul, now blossoming into a new life". The Star in this tail does not foretell; it answers what is already inside. The real comet appeared in 1811, was visible for about 260 days and was called Napoleon's Comet; Tolstoy labelled it with the year it was supposed to foretell. And in 2016 Dave Malloy's musical Natasha, Pierre & The Great Comet of 1812 opened on Broadway: its title holds the whole middle of this tail — two people and a star.

Benebell Wen supplies three more clues. The Star, she writes, "appears chronologically in the Major Arcana after a great deal of pain: The Hanged Man, Death, The Devil, and The Tower", and it means "that the final low point in a situation has passed". In this couple's matrix three of the four stand next to The Star: The Devil at the entry and Death at the centre — always; The Hanged Man in the couple's values — in almost every second couple. Wen also tells two kinds of despair apart: "The Star reversed is about believing that the Seeker won't experience a positive outcome, while The Devil is about believing that no positive outcome can possibly come from such a world." Natasha speaks in the words of The Star: "all is over for me". And the message of the reversed Star, in Wen's words, is "There, there, don't cry." Pierre says almost exactly that: "Stop, stop!"

The second starry night comes in 1813, at Princess Mary's. Natasha tells "what she had never yet mentioned to anyone" about Prince Andrew's last days, "mingling most trifling details with the intimate secrets of her soul". Then Pierre talks about his captivity and wants to pass over the horrors, but "Natásha insisted that he should not omit anything". Two people pour out their stories to each other without measure and without calculation — this is what The Star looks like for this couple.

The middle N is what the couple goes through on the way from the wish to the task. Here the way runs through openness. The two can tell each other something shameful and lose no respect. They talk about a dream while it is still an "if". They back the other's gift even when it eats up the evenings. Lisovskaya writes that under The Star people often discover only within the couple who they want to be. The minus is a picture in place of the truth: a beautiful couple for everyone else, and nobody knows how things really are. The partner is compared with others, treated like a fan, given ultimatums: "it's me or your music". Pierre fears exactly this minus while he waits for Natasha's answer: what if she says that he is "a man, just a man, while I...? I am something altogether different and higher."

This couple's Star is made not from the ends of the tail but from the two personal middles: The Hierophant of one partner (5) and The Hanged Man of the other (12). From the ends, the personal formula would have put Justice in the middle: 15 + 20 = 35 → 8. In the novel it is Pierre who tries to do justice: he stays behind in burning Moscow to kill Napoleon, his beast 666. Nothing comes of it. He saves a stranger's little girl from a fire and is taken prisoner. And there, at a halt by an unharnessed cart, he laughs out loud: "What, me? Me? My immortal soul?" — and looks up at the sky: "And all that is me, all that is within me, and it is all I!" (Tolstoy's Russian begins "all this is mine".)

sections.h2: Main task — Judgement: a judge one chooses
paragraphs: Lisovskaya reads the twentieth energy in a couple through kin and family: relatives, traditions, the influence of parents. The main task D is read mostly through the minus — what the couple struggles with and what it has to learn.

In the novel Judgement arrives as a war. Wen writes that with this card "events currently happening in the Seeker's life will be the catalyst to a personal awakening". The year 1812 burns Moscow and every old form, and the heroes rise from the ashes. Of Natasha Tolstoy says: "She thought her life was ended, but her love for her mother unexpectedly showed her that the essence of life—love—was still active within her. Love awoke and so did life." The awakening comes through the family — through love for her mother, not through a new love. Judgement in the couple's sense is exactly this kind of resurrection: through one's own people.

The same happens to Pierre, only in the language of a court. After captivity "there was now within him a judge who by some rule unknown to him decided what should or should not be done". And when he meets Natasha he feels "that his freedom had also completely gone", that "there was now a judge of his every word and action whose judgment mattered more to him than that of all the rest of the world". This is the turn of the whole tail. At the entry there was "no barrier" and a chain put on him by others. At the end there is freedom given up of his own accord, and a judge he chose himself.

At the same meeting Pierre says of Hélène: "When two people quarrel they are always both in fault, and one's own guilt suddenly becomes terribly serious when the other is no longer alive." To own one's share and not only the other's is, for Lisovskaya, the very task of the twentieth energy; the minus is blaming the partner without seeing one's own part.

And the union is put together by family. Pierre asks Princess Mary for help, and she answers: "Write to her parents, and leave it to me." In the first full draft of the novel Prince Andrew and Petya stay alive — and Natasha still marries Pierre. There Andrew, Sonya and Mary bring the two together themselves, while Natasha wonders uneasily: "What are they doing to me?" (our translation). Tolstoy rewrote who would die, but not who would end up with whom. Among the titles he considered for the novel was All's Well That Ends Well.

In a couple's life the minus of Judgement looks ordinary. The wedding waits for the parents' approval. The holidays are divided between two families, and the couple has none of its own. In an argument someone says "that's how we do things", and it is unclear whose "we" that is. One partner cannot decide anything without phoning their mother. There are no boundaries at all — relatives walk in without knocking — or the boundaries are made of stone and the couple lives in a fortress. The union holds together "for the sake of something": a flat, status, the children. The task is to hear what this family needs now and to write its own laws, taking from the parents' homes only what they want to pass on. On the plus side Lisovskaya notes that a big gap in age, standing or looks does not get in the way of such couples. In Tolstoy that gap is an illegitimate son turned count, in spectacles, and a girl who sang.

sections.h2: Epilogue: where The Devil comes home
paragraphs: Natasha married in the early spring of 1813; by 1820 she has three daughters and a son. And in the epilogue the word from the entry comes back. "The subject which wholly engrossed Natásha's attention was her family: that is, her husband whom she had to keep so that he should belong entirely to her and to the home." Pierre is surprised by her view "that every moment of his life belonged to her and to the family". She is "jealous of Sónya, of the governess, and of every woman, pretty or plain". The general opinion: "Pierre was under his wife's thumb". And at the same time: "At home Natásha placed herself in the position of a slave to her husband." Each is the other's slave.

Tolstoy sees happiness in this, and Waite supplies the key. Of The Devil himself he writes that he is "blind to the liberty of service". The epilogue shows that liberty: each serves the other and the home. After seven years of marriage Pierre "saw himself reflected in his wife", and only the good remained in the reflection — the mirror of The Star. One evening they begin to speak at the same moment, interrupt each other and "both stopped to let the other continue". Their son is called Petya, like Natasha's brother who was killed in 1812: the dead man rises again in a name. And on the last pages Pierre says: "if vicious people are united and constitute a power, then honest folk must do the same". The chain has become an alliance.

But this victory has a price, and it shows in the numbers too. The couple's main task, 20, is always made of one partner's personal Star (17) and the other's Empress (3). In the epilogue that is exactly what happens: "Natásha on the contrary had at once abandoned all her witchery, of which her singing had been an unusually powerful part." The voice went into the nursery, The Star into The Empress, and together they became a family. Natasha is hardly seen in society, and she never speaks of Prince Andrew with her husband. The question this tail asks is whether the Star of one of the two will dissolve in the family or go on shining inside it. Lisovskaya advises such couples not to sacrifice their own work for the partner and not to make the partner choose.

sections.h2: The couple's centre — Death: two people who can talk about endings
paragraphs: At the centre of the couple's matrix with tail 15-17-20 there is always 13, Death. The couple's centre is its shared atmosphere, what lies between the two and is not on show. Death here is not about losses but about what that atmosphere is made of: old forms come to an end between these two people, and they are not afraid to talk about it. Lisovskaya describes such a couple as living proof that life goes on after the hardest things: often it is not a first union, and each accepts the other's past and moves on.

The meeting of Pierre and Natasha in 1813 is almost entirely a conversation about deaths: Petya, Prince Andrew, Hélène, Karataev, the execution Pierre witnessed. They come together over the story of someone else's end, and only afterwards do they laugh: Natasha tells Princess Mary that Pierre "has somehow grown so clean, smooth, and fresh—as if he had just come out of a Russian bath; do you understand? Out of a moral bath." The minus of Death at the centre is an emotional seesaw, a former partner's traits pinned on the present one, and a past nobody talks about. Tolstoy has that too: Natasha never mentions Andrew to her husband, "who she imagined was jealous of Prince Andrew's memory". The dead man becomes a third, silent lodger in the house.

The couple's Death is made of the two personal centres: The Chariot of one partner (7) and The Lovers of the other (6). So The Lovers turn up in both: for one at the entry of the personal tail, for the other at the centre.

sections.h2: The Devil, The Star and Judgement in Waite: a ring, nakedness and a trumpet
paragraphs: On the site the cards have their own artwork; here they are as Waite described them for Pamela Colman Smith's deck. In his Devil "there is a ring in front of the altar, from which two chains are carried to the necks of two figures, male and female". One ring, two chains — the house of Kuragin, which holds both Pierre and Natasha. Wen names the chained pair outright: "The Lovers from Key 6". The one above them, says Waite, "is not to be their master for ever" and is unfree himself; Anatole, it turns out, is secretly married. Among the reversed meanings of The Devil Waite lists "blindness" — think of the spectacles Hélène asks Pierre to take off.

Waite's Star is "entirely naked" and stands for "Truth unveiled". Tolstoy has the opposite nakedness as well. That same evening at the opera, where Natasha is introduced to Anatole, Hélène sits beside her and smiles at everyone in the same way; Tolstoy's word for her is golaya, "naked", which Maude softens to "scantily clad". Nakedness on display, the same for everyone, is the minus of The Star. The nakedness of truth is Natasha insisting that Pierre should not omit anything.

On Waite's Judgement the dead rise from their tombs, and "all the figures are as one in the wonder, adoration and ecstacy expressed by their attitudes". The card, he writes, registers the accomplishment of the great work of transformation in answer to a summons "heard and answered from within". Pierre hears such a summons twice: in captivity, when he laughs at those who have locked up his "immortal soul", and under the comet, which answers what was already in him.

sections.h2: How tail 15-17-20 is calculated: an example couple
paragraphs: The couple's matrix is built from the two personal ones: each of its points is the sum of the same points of the two partners, reduced to 22. The example uses the dates 10.01.1977 and 19.03.1979.
The partners' personal tails are 6-5-17 and 9-12-3. The couple's values in this example are 21, The World.

This is not a one-off. Running through every date shows that tail 15-17-20 is built only one way: one partner has the personal tail 6-5-17, the other 9-12-3, in 100% of couples. That is why all such couples share the same centre, Death. The tail turns up in about one couple in 664 (0.151%), which ranks it 78th of the 97 couple tails.

The middle of a couple's tail is not recalculated from its ends: it is added up from the middles of the two personal tails. The ends would give 15 + 20 = 35 → 8, Justice, but here it is The Star, and in a personal matrix such a middle is impossible. So is the tail itself: in a personal matrix the entry M equals the main task D plus the centre, and with D = 20 no centre gives an entry of 15. This tail exists only for two.

sections.h2: The couple's values: captivity, a globe of drops, or a home
paragraphs: The couple's values are what the union exists for. Tail 15-17-20 has three of them: The Hanged Man (12) in 44.9% of couples, The World (21) in 38.1%, The Empress (3) in 17%. All three are in Tolstoy.

The Hanged Man is Pierre's captivity and what he learns there: "as there is no condition in which man can be happy and entirely free, so there is no condition in which he need be unhappy and lack freedom". A couple with these values holds together because it can look at trouble from the other side.

The World is Pierre's dream after Karataev's death. An old geography teacher shows him a living globe: "Its whole surface consisted of drops closely pressed together", merging and dividing. "That is life." "God is in the midst, and each drop tries to expand so as to reflect Him to the greatest extent." A union that exists for something larger than the two of them is a drop that wants to reflect the whole.

The Empress is the home of the epilogue: children, nursing, a house full to the brim. A simple, earthly value: to make things grow. Such a couple does well to remember that a home is a garden, not a fence.

sections.h2: What helps a couple with tail 15-17-20

ul: **Name the chains out loud.** Each partner arrives with one: an old relationship, a parents' house, an old habit, a debt. They come off through talking, not through closeness.
**Speak about desires before they turn into grievances.** The Devil lives in silence. Saying "I want" is not the same as demanding.
**Keep the "if".** A dream can be spoken before it becomes possible: Pierre said the main thing long before the wedding.
**Tell everything, but freely.** The openness of The Star is a gift, not an interrogation with a phone check.
**In a quarrel, look for your own part first.** "When two people quarrel they are always both in fault."
**Write your own laws.** Decide together which traditions from the parents' homes to take along and which to leave there.
**Don't bury a gift inside the family.** Each partner should keep their own "singing": work, friends, a voice.

**Tell service from a chain.** Service is given out of love, and it can say "no". If "belonging" in the couple has turned into control, threats or fear, this is no longer about cards: it is time for a psychologist, and in danger, a local emergency number.

**Entry to the task — 15, The Devil.** The couple is drawn together by a strong pull and by the wish that nothing should stand between them. The same wish easily turns into a chain: jealousy, control, the habit of holding on.

**Middle of the task — 17, The Star.** The way runs through openness: telling what has never been told to anyone, giving without keeping count, backing the other's gift. The risk is a pretty picture in place of the truth.

**Main task — 20, Judgement.** To build a family of their own with laws of their own: to own their share of the blame, to hear what life asks of them now, and not to live by the script of their parents' homes. The minus is a family that becomes a cage in its own right.

intro: The tail is rare: it turns up in roughly one couple in 664. And it comes with a ready-made plot. Tolstoy told it in War and Peace, in the story of Pierre Bezukhov and Natasha Rostova, and the three cards appear there in exactly this order.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 15-17-20 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's task read in three steps. At the entry is The Devil: the couple is drawn together by a strong pull and the wish to be everything to each other, and that wish can become a chain. In the middle is The Star: the way through openness, unveiled truth and support for the other's gift. The main task is Judgement: to build a family of their own with laws of their own, to own their share of the blame and not to let the family become a cage.

faq.q: Is tail 15-17-20 a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not predict events or pass sentences: it shows where the couple stumbles and what it learns. The Devil here is the entry, not the outcome, and the main card of the tail is Judgement, the card of awakening. In Tolstoy, Pierre and Natasha walk this road, and it ends in a family.

faq.q: Why is The Star in the middle of the tail and not Justice?
faq.a: The middle of a couple's tail is added up from the middles of the two personal tails: The Hierophant of one partner (5) and The Hanged Man of the other (12) give The Star (17). If it were worked out from the ends, as in a personal matrix, the result would be 15 + 20 = 35 → 8, Justice. So the middle of this couple cannot be guessed from the ends: both partners bring it.

faq.q: Can tail 15-17-20 appear in a personal matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the entry M equals the main task D plus the centre, and with a main task of 20 no centre gives an entry of 15. Tail 15-17-20 appears only in a couple's matrix: one partner has the personal tail 6-5-17, the other 9-12-3.

faq.q: Are there couple tails with the same numbers in a different order?
faq.a: No. Among the 97 couple tails the numbers 15, 17 and 20 occur only in the order 15-17-20: The Devil at the entry, The Star in the middle, Judgement as the main task.

The beast, a star and the Apocalypse with its Last Judgement. The Devil, The Star and Judgement — tail 15-17-20 sits whole inside War and Peace. And not only in Pierre's head: the story of Pierre and Natasha runs in exactly this order, and no letters need bending to make it so.

The question this tail asks is **whether the star of one of the two will dissolve in the family or go on shining inside it**.

What helps is simple: naming out loud the chains each partner brought along — an old relationship, a parents' house, an old habit; speaking about desires before they turn into grievances; in a quarrel, looking for one's own part first; leaving each partner their own "singing" — work, friends, a voice. If "belonging" in the couple has turned into control, threats or fear, this is no longer about cards: it is time for a psychologist, and in danger, a local emergency number or crisis line.

unit.title: Who belongs to whom

captions.M: To want closeness with no barriers, and not put on a chain
captions.N: To open up fully and back each other's gift
captions.D: To build your own family, where service is freely given

unit.meaning: Your task is a family with laws of your own, where you belong to each other without chains and no one dims their star.
